ModelCharacter: The highly practical cockpit evolution of the DeFever 44 family: a heavy flush-deck cruiser with single-level walkaround decks, huge aft master, near-standing engine room and five feet of added cockpit for line handling, fishing and water access.
DesignLineage: The DeFever 49 Cockpit Motor Yacht is commonly called the '44+5' because it is based on the DeFever 44 with a five-foot cockpit extension.

ModelCharacter: The fishing/cockpit-oriented 1979–82 sister to the original Mainship 34. It uses the same basic hull and single-diesel philosophy but gives roughly three additional feet to the cockpit at the direct expense of salon length, with a much shorter flybridge and little or no cockpit roof overhang.
DesignLineage: Introduced around 1979 as the cockpit-focused sistership to the original Mainship 34 Diesel Cruiser.
The MK II uses the same basic semi-displacement hull and long keel as the MK I.
Its defining changes are the much larger cockpit, shorter salon, shorter flybridge and little/no aft cabin-top overhang; step-down cockpit gunwales also distinguish many examples.
Both MK I and MK II were replaced by the 34 III for 1983.
OwnershipCharacter: Best suited to owners who value cockpit work space, fishing or outdoor living more than maximum salon room. Mechanical ownership is essentially the same single-diesel/shaft proposition as the MK I; cockpit structure, drains, fuel tanks and deck penetrations deserve age-related inspection.

ModelVariations.Name: Production-location evolution
ModelVariations.Description: Production moved from Taiwan to Nova Scotia after 1992, with reduced exterior teak and interior changes including aft-head and master-berth revisions.

ModelCharacter: A classic Ed Monk Jr.-designed aft-cabin trawler that became one of the most recognizable North American cruising boats of the 1980s and 1990s. Its semi-displacement hull, full skeg/keel protection, single diesel, wide side decks and two-stateroom layout combine simple low-speed economy with unusually comfortable long-term cruising for 36 feet.
DesignLineage: Ed Monk Jr., not Ed Monk Sr., designed the Monk 36; the two naval architects worked together for many years, which likely contributes to recurring attribution confusion.
Production began in Taiwan in 1982 and shifted to Nova Scotia in 1992 while retaining the same essential hull and galley-up aft-cabin arrangement.
The post-1992 Canadian-built generation reduced exterior teak, eliminated the aft-head bathtub and improved the aft master berth placement.
Production continued through 2007, with more than 250 boats reported built over roughly 25 years.
OwnershipCharacter: One of the simpler 36-foot liveaboard trawlers to operate: normally one shaft-drive diesel, straightforward systems, secure walkaround decks and strong owner knowledge. Early Taiwan boats carry much more exterior teak and may have older Lehman/Perkins installations; later Nova Scotia boats reduce wood maintenance but often add more powerful Cummins machinery and modern cruising systems.

ModelVariations.Name: 28 versus 38 mission difference
ModelVariations.Description: The NP28 is a compact pilothouse pocket trawler; the NP38 Sedan is a larger Europa-style cruiser with substantially greater displacement and tankage.

ModelCharacter: A purpose-built pocket trawler that combines a legal-width 8'6" beam, raised pilothouse, warm teak interior and single Cummins shaft drive in a genuinely transportable package. It cruises efficiently at 6–8 knots but uses a modified semi-displacement version of Karl Stambaugh's original full-displacement concept to reach roughly 10–13 knots when needed.
DesignLineage: North Pacific Yachts was founded in 2004 by John and Trevor Brice; the 28 became the company's third model.
Trevor Brice developed the NP28 after seeing Karl Stambaugh's Trailer Trawler 28 concept in Passagemaker in 2007.
Stambaugh's original concept was full displacement; North Pacific modified the hull slightly to semi-displacement to increase maximum speed.
The first China-built NP28 hull arrived in 2009, establishing a distinct compact branch below North Pacific's larger pilothouse and sedan cruisers.
OwnershipCharacter: A strong owner-operator design with single-shaft diesel propulsion, bow thruster, excellent machinery access for the size and little exterior wood. Trailerability is real in beam, but total rig weight, length and height demand serious tow equipment rather than casual SUV trailering.

ModelCharacter: A compact early-1990s aft-cabin yacht designed to fit two private staterooms, two heads with stall showers, salon, dinette and galley into a nominal 34-foot class. Its actual overall length approaches 40 feet, reflecting the aft deck, pulpit and swim-platform-heavy motor-yacht architecture.
DesignLineage: The Silverton 34 Motor Yacht was produced from 1993–1996.
It predates Silverton's later SideWalk motor yachts and uses more conventional side-deck/aft-deck circulation.
The model established Silverton's maxi-volume small-motor-yacht theme before the 352 arrived in 1997.
The later 352 is not a renamed 34; it is a much larger, SideWalk-based design.
OwnershipCharacter: Twin gas inboards are conventional and broadly serviceable, but packaging is dense and storage is limited. Two heads, hardtop, bridge, wet bar and nearly 40-foot actual LOA create costs closer to a larger yacht than the '34' badge suggests.

ModelCharacter: Silverton's first successful double-cabin design, introduced in 1982 with a wide 14-foot beam, shallow keel, two private staterooms and full-width aft deck. It established the affordable, high-volume aft-cabin formula that later Silverton motor yachts refined.
DesignLineage: The Silverton 40 Aft Cabin was introduced in 1982 and produced through 1990.
It was Silverton's first double-cabin design and became a strong sales success.
Interior joinery changed from teak to lighter oak beginning with 1985 models.
Later Silverton aft-cabin/SideWalk motor yachts evolved the same high-volume mission with more radical deck architecture.
OwnershipCharacter: A conventional, understandable 1980s motor yacht with twin gas inboards and large but simple domestic spaces. Fuel consumption, two-head plumbing, aft-deck canvas/hardtop, aging tanks and original wiring are the main ownership burdens; the shallow keel helps directional stability but does not make it a trawler.
